documents.t: I looked up some Level 1 problems I’d solved more than a year ago. Back then their solve rates had been low. They’d gone up quite a bit since. I figured the same thing had happened with Hide the Cactus. I really should’ve left that one alone…

I’ll reconstruct the problem roughly from memory. Absolutely nothing to do with being afraid to look at it again. 1 <= m, n <= 500_000 1 <= m x n <= 500_000 Given those constraints, even a loop over m with a loop over n inside it would stay within a reasonable bound. “Well, I can just brute-force this,” I thought. Then my very humble solution (does it count as a solution if I never solved it?) grew to four nested loops, and suddenly I was looking at 250_000_000_000. “I’ll come up with something so ingenious even Ludens will fall over backwards.” I turned it over every which way. What actually fell into a ditch was two hours of my time. I tried an easier Kakao problem after that. I don’t know. The problem itself seemed fine. My head and whatever was going on inside it were another story. One more failed attempt, and then the eleven o’clock ride home from campus. Where did my time go?

Ludens looked through a few blogs and told me this one called for a monotonic queue. I’ve done a few monotonic stack problems before. I wonder how much carries over? A few more stack problems, and next week I’ll come back and give that cactus what for. Original post on Rilog (Korean)

Actually, the hamburger can’t keep me company. I’ve already devoured it without mercy. Then again, maybe it’s closer to me now than it was before I ate it. What does it matter, anyway? It’s 2:50 in the morning. Wednesday, October 7. I’m at the McDonald’s by Sunae Station. There’s something reassuring about a chain that stays open all night. Even when I’m away from home, there’s somewhere I can stay, whatever the hour. Why am I awake at this hour? And why am I here when I have a perfectly cozy home? Well, here you’ve found me, writing about The Stranger. I figured if I was going to work through the small hours anyway, I might as well get something to eat and give myself a change of scenery. I hadn’t actually set out to write about The Stranger. I did have to write it eventually. A few of us at Woowacourse had read the book and got together to talk about it, and we’d agreed to bring something we’d written to follow up. But just before I started this, I was making a list of things I’d done, for my application to an entry-level opening at MyRealTrip. Then a couple of thoughts occurred to me. Looking back over my time at Woowacourse for the application, I could see a resemblance between MyRealTrip and our project. In both, the starting point was the problem we wanted to solve. If I got the job, what could I do at MyRealTrip with the things I already love? I like books. I have a soft spot for films, music, other books, food, even places, once I’ve come across them in a book. Japanese fiction does this to me in particular. People travel around taking photos of places they’ve seen in anime. What if you could plan a route that let you visit places you’d read about, or try the food? I remember reading Haruki Murakami’s After Dark and jotting down the things that turned up in it in the back of my copy. A lot of it was music. It was fun. It made me want to build a little wiki of my own as I went through life. I like running. Travel abroad has never stirred much in me either way. Lately, though, just picturing myself out for a run overseas makes my heart swell. And a good running route is hard to plan. Especially a long one. There are only so many laps of a track you can do before it gets old. It’s tricky enough at home, so I imagine it would be harder in another country. What if we could map out routes in enough detail for people to go running with peace of mind? As you can probably tell from all that rambling, I got quite excited at the thought of where MyRealTrip was headed and how much fun I might have there. Forming hypotheses, making decisions with data, seeing something through from start to finish even when it took me outside my area. I’d made a point of practicing all that at Woowacourse. I could almost believe those experiences had come my way specifically for MyRealTrip. And then there’s this. Would another company recognize what I’m writing down here? Would they see any value in it? The other backend developers in my cohort seem to be preparing for their applications in a rather different way. Am I a stranger on the job market? Getting as far as that question is the beginning and the end of this book report. It’s a question that worries me. It makes me anxious. It’s a challenge, too. I’ve got all these names for the situation, and I don’t know quite what to do with any of them. Even this is a hypothesis. It needs testing. The weight of it is rather different from that of a hypothesis in a project or a survey. A good deal heavier. Still, it’s mine to bear. Is this life? Good. Then I’ll do it again. I’ve written a book report without saying what happens in The Stranger. Yet I feel closer to Meursault now than I did when I still had the whole book fresh in my head, scribbling in the margins about what a scene was doing or what a sentence stood for. The way I used to read was to get a feel for the people in a book, for the time they lived in, and to enjoy being there. People say books let you learn about other people’s lives. And yet, as far as Meursault’s own life goes, I feel further away from it now. I don’t know what the book is about. I don’t know what it’s about, but right now, I’m a stranger.
Original post on Rilog (Korean)

documents.t: Was it two or three weeks ago? For some reason I woke early and went for a run along the Tancheon. Dawn had passed, but the sunlight still looked blue. I’d run an easy two kilometers or so and was heading back up. The paved ramp was broad enough for maintenance vehicles. Most of the time a metal barrier keeps them out, leaving just enough of a gap for one person to pass. [Photo of the ramp goes here] I’d just finished my run and was puffing my way uphill. Behind me came a middle-aged man who looked as though he’d been out for a leisurely walk. As I reached the top, another middle-aged man on a bicycle went past me in the opposite direction. He looked a little younger than the man coming up. They were both heading for the same gap. Only one could get through at a time. The man coming uphill was looking at his phone, and it seemed to fall to the cyclist to do enough dodging for the pair of them, in rather a hurry. He must have steered well, because they didn’t collide. He did mutter a startled “Ah, damn it” on his way down. For all his attention to the phone, the other man heard that part perfectly well. “Hey! What did you just say?” Their voices rose. ... Watching them, I felt sorry for them both. I’m grateful whenever I get to go outside and enjoy the morning air. A surprising number of things have to come together for me to do it, from going to bed early the night before to getting past the urge to spend five more minutes under the covers. All that, spoiled for want of a moment’s patience. I wondered whether they’d spend the day complaining about each other to their families, or replaying it alone and getting upset all over again. Original post on Rilog (Korean)

Ordinary Twig. A perfectly ordinary-looking twig made through alchemy. It doesn’t seem to have any special powers. (Image source) ↳ And there’s my weapon. My history shows I was solving problems until about the summer of 2025. After that, nothing. Back to square zero, then?

Apparently I solved some in JS, too. Was that when I was preparing for Naver Boostcamp? I remember how exciting it felt just to be using a new language. At the time, the missions that landed every day were so… incredibly… hard. I was forever staying up all night and crashing at four in the afternoon. I was a wreck. Funny how many good memories I have of it now.

documents.t: import java.util.*; class Solution { // A runner’s name is called when they overtake someone. public String[] solution( String[] players, // Runners in their current order, starting with first place String[] callings // Names in the order they are called ) { Map<String, Integer> playerOrderMap = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < players.length; i++) { playerOrderMap.put(players[i], i); } // 1. Call a name. for (String calling : callings) { int order = playerOrderMap.get(calling); // Runner in second, for example String temp = players[order-1]; // Runner in first players[order-1] = players[order]; // Move the second runner into first. players[order] = temp; // Move the former leader into second. playerOrderMap.put(calling, order - 1); // Overtook playerOrderMap.put(temp, order); // Was overtaken } // Names in finishing order, from first through nth return players; } }

At first I skipped the Map and tried for (String calling : callings) { brute-force : players }. It timed out. So far, fine. I suspected I’d need a map anyway. A quick solution I expected to fail would tell me whether I was approaching the problem the right way. Where I went wrong​ Then I kept getting the swap wrong. All I wanted to do was use temp to exchange the runners in positions n and n−1. playerOrderMap.put(calling, order - 1); // Overtook // Fix: temp still holds the runner who occupied [order-1]. playerOrderMap.put(temp, order); // Was overtaken // Bug: [order-1] has already changed, but I treated it as if it still held the previous runner. // playerOrderMap.put(players[order-1], order); I’d written playerOrderMap.put(players[order-1], order) where I needed playerOrderMap.put(temp, order). The original runner in position n−1 dropped out of the ordering, and the runner from position n appeared twice. Maybe I was rusty. I had to print the whole thing out before I could see it. kai overtakes poe # bug: poe disappears and kai appears twice Current order: mumu,soe,kai,kai,mine, kai overtakes kai # bug: kai disappears and mine appears twice Current order: mumu,soe,kai,kai,mine, mine overtakes kai Current order: mumu,soe,kai,mine,mine, mine overtakes mine Current order: mumu,soe,kai,mine,mine, Something for next time​ There’s a Duck in our group who’s suspiciously good at these problems. I had a peek at their solution. While I was losing track of what temp, players[order], and players[order-1] stood for, Duck had a variable called frontName. I liked that word, front. It told me who was standing where. Duck did say nice things about my solution. Whether that was praise or a way to fish a drowning newbie out by the collar and keep them from escaping the group… I’m still not sure. Original post on Rilog (Korean)

1. YTN reports a heavy rain advisory for Seoul and Gyeonggi. 2. The same advisory on KBS. It’s a Sunday in the autumn of 2026, and the rain is coming down hard. By about six in the evening, though, it was letting up. I started getting my running things together. Down at the Tancheon, you could see what the rain had done. The water was just shy of covering the stepping stones between the two banks. 3. The stepping stones, just above water. As if the stream had decided it couldn’t hold much more, the current was picking up, carrying the water off to some place far away. 4. All that water rushing downstream. I was admiring the way water could flow quietly or pick up speed as the occasion called for it, when something I’d heard once came back to me. A lot of our technology comes from watching what nature does. It matters to me to have some breathing room in my life. But when things need doing, maybe I can let the current run a little faster for a while. Like water. So I’ve decided to be water. With so little of my time at Woowacourse left, I think I’m going to need a fairly brisk current. 5. Biomimetics, on Wikipedia. 6. Today’s run.
Last time I ran here I saw raccoon dogs and a bird. I wonder how they fared today. 7. Raccoon dog A. 8. Raccoon dog B. 9. A bird. Asleep, perhaps? 10. A closer look.

This essay suggests a way to take pleasure in adversity. Several passages circle the same idea, so I’ll finish by gathering them here. The excerpts below are translated from the Korean edition. The good things of prosperity are worth wishing for. The good things of adversity are worth admiring. — Seneca I’ve been seeing a Korean collection of Seneca for people who feel today slipping away everywhere lately. It was a surprise to run into him in Francis Bacon, too. Surely, if miracles have power over nature, it’s in adversity that they tend to appear. The virtue of prosperity is temperance, and the virtue of adversity is fortitude. Of the two, fortitude is by far the more heroic. Prosperity is the blessing of the Old Testament. Adversity is the blessing of the New. It promises greater grace and reveals God’s protection more clearly. Even in adversity there is comfort and hope. In needlework or embroidery, how much more pleasing to set a lively pattern against a grave, somber ground than to lay a dark, melancholy pattern on a bright one. Prosperity brings our vices into view. Adversity brings out our virtues.
documents.s: Reading Bacon’s “Of Adversity” in the Moonye edition

documents.t: Holy Spirit, also Holy Ghost. It’s a Christian term. Even with an explanation in front of me, I find it hard to grasp. I’ve seen Christians in Korea and elsewhere writing about their own confusion over it, too. The pen of the Holy Spirit also dwells more on the afflictions of Job than on the splendor of Solomon. Needlework. Making something by hand, sometimes with the help of a simple tool. In needlework or embroidery, to set a lively pattern against a grave, somber ground… Original post on Rilog (Korean)

documents.t: Volume one of Haruki Murakami’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. Volume one of The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, from an Aladin secondhand bookshop. I got it secondhand for 4,900 won. Isn’t that ridiculously cheap? I was happy. What made me happier still was that it was a well-aged book. Tucked inside was a postcard that expired in 2008. Oh, and I bought a fabric book cover. Was it 10,800 won?

Here’s where things went awry. Two beeps from the scanner, and the cashier said: “If you spend 20,000 won, you get 3,000 won off. Shall I ring these up as they are?” This happened last time, too. Buying more to get the discount would cost me more than skipping it, I thought. “Just these, please.” And then I went home.

Why was it that today I heard myself say, “Oh, then I’ll have another look around.” Where did that come from? Off I went to find a book that would bring me up to the threshold. If I was buying one, I wanted one I actually cared about. English and American fiction, Japanese fiction, popular science, the Minumsa World Literature shelves… I drifted from section to section. Nothing. Nothing I felt drawn to. It’s hot in Aladin. I was wearing long sleeves, a lightweight puffer, and a trench coat. The trench coat had long since ended up over my arm. I thought my arm might give out if I added the puffer, so I wandered around with it half off, flapping behind me. Half off, half overheated. My arm was heavy, and the rest of me was starting to feel it. Still no book. I’d already sunk ten minutes into this. I finally took the puffer all the way off and browsed in slightly more comfort, but my body had already got the message. And so, suddenly worn out, I picked up Julian Barnes’s Departure(s) and trudged home. The book I finally settled on, Departure(s) by Julian Barnes. When I pick a book, something about the title and the author’s name has to catch me on sight. It has to look cool to me. This title is so much my sort of thing that I’d had my eye on it for ages. How did it take me that long to spot it? When I started writing this I was still thinking, what a waste of a trip to the bookshop. Now I’m looking at my two books and I feel rather pleased. Maybe it does come down to where you choose to end the story. Original post on Rilog (Korean)

What you’ll take away How a view and a snapshot explain the difference between an unmodifiable collection and an immutable one. How the lists produced by these calls differ: Collections.unmodifiableList() List.of() or List.copyOf() Calling a mutating method throws an UnsupportedOperationException.
documents.s: Unmodifiable Lists and Immutable Lists in Java

documents.t: The UnmodifiableRandomAccessList implementation (which I’ll call UnmodifiableList here) is a view of the original collection. As the code below shows, it holds the original list in a field. For a read like get, the wrapper delegates to the corresponding method on that list and returns the result. Say x001 refers to the original list and x002 to the view. You can call add through x001. Trying it through x002 throws. A change made through x001 also shows up through x002, since the wrapper still holds that same list. static class UnmodifiableList<E> extends UnmodifiableCollection<E> implements List<E> { final List<? extends E> list; UnmodifiableList(List<? extends E> list) { super(list); this.list = list; } ... public E get(int index) {return list.get(index);} public void add(int index, E element) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } ... } You can try it in this example.

This list captures the contents of the original collection at the moment of the copy. Later structural changes to the original list don’t affect it. // List.java ... static <E> List<E> copyOf(Collection<? extends E> coll) { return ImmutableCollections.listCopy(coll); } ... // ImmutableCollections.java ... static <E> List<E> listCopy(Collection<? extends E> coll) { ... } else { // Copy the elements into a collection independent of the original. return (List<E>)List.of(coll.toArray()); } } ...

I left out a branch earlier to keep the example manageable. Here’s the full body of ImmutableCollections.listCopy(). Look at the first if. static <E> List<E> listCopy(Collection<? extends E> coll) { // List12 and ListN both extend AbstractImmutableList. // For these compatible immutable lists, copyOf can return the input itself. if (coll instanceof List12 || (coll instanceof ListN<?> c && !c.allowNulls)) { return (List<E>)coll; // The remaining branches handle other inputs. } else if (coll.isEmpty()) { return List.of(); } else { return (List<E>)List.of(coll.toArray()); } } You can also find this in the Javadoc’s implementation note: Implementation Note: If the given Collection is an unmodifiable List, calling copyOf will generally not create a copy. In the next example, compare the references. For this immutable list, List.copyOf returns the same object. The last example times repeated calls with the same immutable input. There’s no copying to do, and the elapsed time shown in this run is 0 ms.
documents.s: 3. When List.copyOf() can return the list it was given

documents.t: We often say that we call a method. Seen through the lens of object-oriented programming, a more precise description of what the sender does is send a message. I learned this in Java, a statically typed language, where the two are easy to conflate. Comparing it with JavaScript helped me see the distinction.
documents.s: Sending a Message and Calling a Method

documents.t: // The return type, name, and parameters are part of the declaration. In discussing the interface, we’ll refer to the operation and its signature. public void sayHello(String name) { // The body supplies the implementation, also called the method. System.out.println("안녕 " + name + "!"); }

Java is statically typed. The compiler checks the type at compile time. When the sender tries to send a message, the receiver’s declared type has to expose the corresponding operation. Otherwise, the program never gets to send it. Compilation fails. Working in a language like Java, it’s easy to come away thinking that sending a message and calling a method are the same thing.
documents.s: 1. Java checks types before the program runs

documents.t: JavaScript is dynamically typed. There’s no compile-time check that a sayHello() method exists on the receiver. You can try sending the message to a rock object that has no such method. Ordinarily, trying to call it will then fail at runtime.

It’s hard to explain the next example as a call to a method on rock. There’s no sayHello() implementation sitting on that object. The message model makes it easier to follow. The sender sends a message named sayHello. The receiver intercepts it and decides how to respond at runtime.
documents.s: A receiver can even respond without defining the named method

documents.t: Objects, Cho Young-ho, p. 49.
SQ3R is a way to study as you read. The idea is to read deliberately, coming up with your own questions and looking for answers as you go.

I used the sources below to put together an account of what SQ3R is and how to try it. I first encountered it in Growing Together, by Kim Chang-joon. Lately I’ve wanted to get better at picking up new things quickly and effectively, so I decided to look into it and give it a try.
Hold off on reading the text itself. Look at the contents, titles, and subheadings to get a sense of the whole.

Write down questions about anything you couldn’t understand or anticipate during the survey. For instance, what might a chapter called “The Programming Language Master” cover? Will it just tell me how good the expert is? Will they share how they got there? What would I have to do to get that good myself? note Reading with your own questions in mind gives you somewhere to direct your attention.
Highlight or annotate the passages that bear on the questions you picked out. Give your eyes something to come back to.

After reading the parts that address a question, try answering it out loud in your own words. With a bit of luck, your reading has given you what you need. Make a note of any questions you struggle to answer. You’ll use them in the last step.

Go back through the questions you wrote down earlier. Keep the questions physically separate from what you read. Quiz cards are one way to do it. With the questions and the text side by side, you can pick up clues without noticing and mistake recognition for knowing the answer. Give yourself the harder job of pulling it out of memory. After all, you generally can’t look it up during an exam! (Well, there are open-book exams…)
Growing Together, by Kim Chang-joon, the chapter on mastering a programming language SQ3R - Harvard Univ.

As he saw it, she hadn’t reproached him because she didn’t want anything to dilute the complete indifference she’d shown him, an indifference that had seemed quite genuine. — F. Scott Fitzgerald, “Winter Dreams,” translated here from the Korean edition I don’t linger over books. I tend to skim along by feel, with no particular ambition to understand a book in its entirety. Every so often, though, I catch myself slowing down. 〰️〰️ It happened when I came across the idea that indifference could fade. It stayed with me enough that I even wrote down a thought about it. The note I left on Chaekchaek about fading indifference. Think of something you’re indifferent to. Perhaps you’ve never even noticed your indifference. A tissue fluttering in the air conditioning at a restaurant, say, or a gray ball of dust on the floor beside your desk. Then there’s a moment when that indifference wears thin. The fluttering tissue suddenly starts to bother you. Someone walks past and the little ball of dust goes skittering off, and your eyes follow it… 〰️〰️ I wonder if it’s the same with people. Maybe what I feel first is my indifference fading. 〰️〰️ Fading indifference. The end. Original post on Rilog (Korean)
documents.s: When Indifference Fades | Fitzgerald’s Winter Dreams

Was it five days ago? I bought the Moonye edition of Francis Bacon’s essays. I knew his line about knowledge being power, and that was about all I knew of him. I happened upon the book and wanted to get better acquainted. My other reason was the size of the essays. There are nearly sixty subjects in some 270 pages. One a day sounded like a pleasant little habit. https://www.yes24.com/product/goods/147564050
documents.s: Francis Bacon on Having No Cause for Anger

documents.t: Who does another person harm just for the pleasure of doing harm? People do it for some gain or pleasure or honor of their own. Why, then, should I be angry with someone for loving himself more than he loves me? — Francis Bacon, “Of Revenge,” translated here from the Korean edition It reminded me of the saying that if you expect nothing, you won’t get angry. But suppose someone has a bad habit, and I keep quiet because, well, it’s their loss. Isn’t that also a failure to communicate? If we care about each other’s growth, wouldn’t it be better to say something? Bacon stops at “there’s no need to get angry.” He doesn’t offer an alternative like “keep calm and talk it through.” I’m left wondering how much he includes under anger. Does it cover telling someone off in a temper and giving them ordinary feedback? If I read it that broadly, I’m back where I started. Staying quiet could end up hurting us both.
documents.s: No cause to be angry with someone?

documents.t: Gomaehada (고매하다). To be distinguished or noble in character, learning, or talent. By comparison, the spirit of Job speaks in a nobler voice. Proverbs. The biblical book numbered 24th or 20th, depending on the ordering. Solomon is traditionally credited with writing or compiling many of its sayings. These are the names in different languages. I take the word to mean something like a maxim or a piece of counsel. Hebrew משלי (Mishlei) Greek Παροιμίαι (Paroimiai) Latin Proverbia English Proverbs Korean 잠언 (箴言), literally “words that prick like a needle”

documents.t: Define the print(String format, Object... args) helper below and use it wherever you want to inspect a value. // Example 1 print("Can move? now=%s(%d, %d)%n", mat[x][tempY], x, tempY); print("Move allowed! now=%s(%d, %d)%n", mat[x][tempY], x, tempY); print("Move (Y): %d -> %d%n", y, tempY); // Example 2 print("=== step %d (start_%s) | oper_%s ===%n", count++, start, oper); public static final boolean DEBUG_MODE = false; private static void print(String format, Object... args) { if (DEBUG_MODE) System.out.printf(format, args); }

I kept getting my bearings wrong at first: how far did I need to search, and from which starting point? I wanted to see the intermediate results, so I started with plain System.out.println() calls. I soon got tired of typing the same output method over and over and joining strings with + just to inspect a value. I wrote print() to take care of both. private static void print(String format, Object... args) { System.out.printf(format, args); } A short helper takes care of typing the same method repeatedly. printf() and the varargs parameter Object... args take care of assembling debug messages with string concatenation.

public static char[][] mat = new char[55][55]; public static int ROW_SIZE; public static int COL_SIZE; public int[] solution( String[] park, // Each cell contains S, O, or X. String[] routes // Commands for the dog, in the form "op n": direction and number of squares ) { ROW_SIZE = park.length - 1; COL_SIZE = park[0].length() - 1; Pos start = new Pos(); print("<ROW_SIZE=%d, COL_SIZE=%d>%n", ROW_SIZE, COL_SIZE); for (int row = 0; row < ROW_SIZE + 1; row++) { for (int col = 0; col < COL_SIZE + 1; col++) { char target = park[row].charAt(col); mat[row][col] = target; if (target == 'S') start = new Pos(row, col); } } for (int row = 0; row < ROW_SIZE + 1; row++) { for (int col = 0; col < COL_SIZE + 1; col++) { print("%s ", mat[row][col]); } print("%n"); } int count = 1; for (String oper : routes) { print("=== step %d (start_%s) | oper_%s ===%n", count++, start, oper); if (start.canMoveTo(oper)) { start.move(oper); } } int[] answer = {start.x, start.y}; // Dog’s final position after all commands: [row, column] return answer; } Original post on Rilog (Korean)
Inflearn picked me for its end-of-year award for answering questions! Yes, that’s me. I’d like to share this award with the production team, who worked so hard, and with… well, you know the speech.

I didn’t even know Inflearn had end-of-year awards. When an email came asking for my address, I took it for one of their regular promotional emails and went right past it. Luckily for me, someone at Inflearn thought to follow up by text. I got my address in after all. And what arrived? Wine and cheese! Just the thing for us grown-up kids studying hard on Inflearn.
documents.s: How the gift found its way to me

documents.t: I learn a surprising amount from answering other people’s questions. And I enjoy the answering itself. There’s quite a distance between knowing something and helping someone else understand it. Sometimes I wonder how well I know a thing if I can only explain it to myself. I’ve often started typing with a cheerful “Oh, I know this one! Let me explain,” only to stop halfway through. “I’ve always taken this bit for granted. How would I explain it to this person?” Or, “Is that actually true? Where does the official documentation say so?” That’s the weight of telling someone how something works. To finish the answer, I have to put what I know into words someone else can follow and find evidence for it. In the process I fill in gaps I hadn’t realized were there.
documents.s: Why did I start answering questions?

documents.t: I already liked Inflearn and was happy using it. I can hardly pretend an end-of-year present hasn’t made me a little fonder of it. Inflearn gave me a chance to leave them a message, so I tried to fit all that affection into it. I’ll leave it here to close out the post. A note to Inflearn​ I had no idea you did anything like this. What a lovely way to end the year! For the past couple of months I’ve been at the Baemin bootcamp, working on the fundamentals as I prepare to look for a job. I haven’t been on Inflearn as much, so it was lovely to be included on the strength of the answers I’d been posting before that. I kept volunteering answers for two reasons. Writing them helped me, and I thought someone might get as much out of mine as I’d gotten out of other people’s. Other students’ answers have often left me with a new question. Chasing it down helped me grow, and sometimes one answer gave me a way of seeing something that hadn’t occurred to me at all. I started answering to return a little of that kindness. Of course, having to explain something to someone else helped me work on my own weak spots, too. Inflearn was there when I first started learning to program. I’m pretty attached to it. Over the last few years I’ve watched the mobile app get updates, new features arrive, and events come and go. I catch myself thinking, “They’re really working at this. Look how much room they still have to grow.” It makes me oddly proud. I’ve found every course I needed on Inflearn. I haven’t even signed up for another service, though I think there are two or three others in Korea. I’m not sure what you currently offer new members. A generous welcome offer might be worth a try. Once people start taking courses, I can see them sticking around. Another way to reach new students might be to get in touch with university administrators or student councils and set up a little campus booth with courses or coupons to give away. They’re in different businesses, but Notion recruits student ambassadors, and I’ve often seen Monster giving away energy drinks on campus. Another thought as I write this: if a few instructors were interested, perhaps Inflearn could approach a university about hosting a guest lecture. I can imagine that going over quite well. This has turned into a long note. I hope you have a lovely end to the year, and that in 2026 both Inflearn and I get a little closer to the things we’re working toward!

A man with a wife and children has given hostages to fortune. In good undertakings and bad alike, they are a great hindrance to anyone who would do great things. — Francis Bacon, “Of Marriage and Single Life,” translated here from the Moonye edition Quite a provocative thing to say. Would I really concentrate harder on my work if I had no children? Couldn’t the responsibility of having a child give me a reason to concentrate harder? It’s exam season at university. I walk into the library determined to pull an all-nighter. It’s ten in the evening, and my computer simulation class starts at two the next afternoon. Sixteen whole hours. Finishing just one chapter every three hours will do nicely. 〰️〰️ Do those sixteen hours I’ve conjured up by staying awake all belong to me? 〰️〰️ And would every hour freed up by having no children be an hour I could spend concentrating? I doubt it. As I was saying, having a child might help me settle into something more deeply and do it well. Though if we’re talking about a newborn who wakes, sleeps, cries, and fusses at all hours and completely wrecks my sleep… well, that would be hard. I like children, but I don’t consciously go around thinking, “I need a wife and kids.” Maybe a child is someone who comes along in the course of living, one more person to share the journey with. If I did share my life with a child, I’d want to meet them as an equal. Another whole person living a life like mine and utterly different from it. That feels a little different from being what people call “a parent who’s like a friend.” 〰️〰️ Parent | Child | Lover | Friend | Teacher Different, and much the same. 〰️〰️ Original post on Rilog (Korean)
documents.s: A Wife and Children Are a Great Hindrance to Great Undertakings

documents.t: I’m ending the day with a teabag of fish-cake broth. Anyone at Woowacourse could tell you that Elephant, yours truly, doesn’t like fish cake. Especially fish-cake soup. And yet today is the sort of day I want to end with that teabag. Does Elephant actually like fish cake? To be remembered, to accomplish something, to do noble deeds: these belong to human beings. The noblest works and foundations have come from people without children. Having no image of their bodies to leave behind, they strive to give expression to an image of their minds. — From the Korean edition I liked the way Bacon starts with the animal instinct to continue a line. If you don’t satisfy it by leaving descendants, an image of your body, he suggests you’ll try to leave an image of your mind. Having a child is a great thing in itself. It can change what you live for and what you hope to do. And surely it changes how you divide up your hours? People often marry around the time they’re coming into their own physically and at work. If they put marriage aside and poured those hours into their work or research, I can imagine more of what Bacon calls an image of the mind surviving them. Then again, the longer you wait for the right time to marry, the more tempted you are to hold out for the best time. Maybe there’s something to marrying when you still don’t feel ready. Parents would do well to choose their children’s occupations and paths early, when the children are still adaptable. It is possible to defer too much to their preferences in the belief that they should do whatever they please. Where a child shows a remarkable inclination or talent, of course, it is best to let it have its way. Does he mean that if parents choose early, the child gets to try something sooner and has less to lose by trying something else if it doesn’t fit? I’m going by that bit about being adaptable. I’m finding this one difficult. Original post on Rilog (Korean)
documents.s: Does Elephant Actually Like Fish Cake? Reading Bacon on Parents and Children

What you’ll take away How mapping data between DTOs can involve translating between two different API contracts. Where to translate external data, and when it makes sense to move that work closer to the external system.
documents.s: [Backend] Integrating an External API Means Translating Its Contract

documents.t: Chaekchaek uses Aladin’s Search API to look up books. From the outset, we had one data transfer object (DTO) for the response we received from Aladin and another for the response we returned to our client. Aladin Search API ↓ (enter our backend) AladinSearchResponse ↓ BookSearchResponse ↓ (leave our backend) Chaekchaek Client On paper, that gives the two APIs a clean separation. Yet fields from Aladin’s pagination model showed up in our public response almost word for word. public record BookSearchResponse( int totalResults, int startIndex, int itemsPerPage, boolean hasNext, List<BookItem> items ) { } We had two objects, but our public contract still reflected the way Aladin represented its data. A client using Chaekchaek should only have to learn Chaekchaek’s contract. Splitting the DTOs had left that part of the job unfinished.
documents.s: 1. Do separate DTOs make us independent of the external API?

documents.t: Even two providers offering the same book search can describe a result quite differently. Meaning Aladin Another provider Search results item documents Authors author: String, including contributor roles authors: String[] Translators Included in author translators: String[] Next page Calculated from pagination fields A separate flag such as is_end The differences go deeper than field names. Providers decide how to divide the same information into fields and how to represent state. Each model makes sense in its own context. Aladin has a model for its service, and Chaekchaek needs one for ours. In practice, we made three kinds of translation. We adopted our own terms. For the number of books found, totalResults became totalCount. We gave loosely structured data a shape our client could use. One string containing authors and translators became a separate array for each role. We turned the provider’s state into the client’s next action. The current page number helped us work out which page to request next. The last two in particular required a decision about which information matters to our service.
documents.s: 2. The provider and our service speak different languages

documents.t: That raises a fair question. If our service needs authors and translators separately, why don’t we split them as soon as we receive the response? Do we really need both AladinSearchResponse and BookSearchResponse? Technically, we could do that. I’d still keep a DTO specifically for Aladin’s response. If you’re familiar with SOLID, the single responsibility principle gives a good reason. Consider what would make us change each model: AladinSearchResponse changes → when Aladin changes its API contract Chaekchaek’s search result model changes → when Chaekchaek’s requirements change Those are two different responsibilities. Keeping them separate gives us somewhere to absorb a change in Aladin’s API before it reaches our clients.
documents.s: 3. The external DTO keeps the provider’s vocabulary

documents.t: Two parts of the implementation made this especially clear.

Aladin puts authors and translators in a single string: 앤디 위어 (지은이), 박아람 (옮긴이) Here, 지은이 marks the author and 옮긴이 marks the translator. Our client needs to use those roles separately: { "authors": ["앤디 위어"], "translators": ["박아람"] } I wrote an AladinContributorParser to interpret the string. Along the way I found a case where splitting on commas would give the wrong answer: 민관식 (필명, 청원) (지은이) The comma inside the parentheses introduces a pen name. It doesn’t separate two contributors. We had to interpret Aladin’s conventions to get a structure Chaekchaek could use. That also meant deciding what to keep. Suppose our service uses only authors and translators and drops illustrators (그림), editorial supervisors (감수), and compilers (엮은이). That’s a product decision, too. The information we allow a translation to lose is part of our policy.
documents.s: 4.1. Turning contributor credits into structured data

documents.t: Aladin describes pagination with three fields: totalResults startIndex itemsPerPage At first, we exposed those fields alongside hasNext. To fetch another page, the client had to know the rule: const nextPage = hasNext ? startIndex + 1 : null; Our server already understood Aladin’s pagination model. It made sense to do the calculation there. That gave us a simpler public response: public record BookSearchResponse( int totalCount, Integer nextPage, List<BookItem> items ) { } The client can now use the value of nextPage directly: nextPage = 3 → Request page 3 next. nextPage = null → There are no more pages. The distinction between these fields is easy to miss. hasNext describes the current state. nextPage gives the client the value it needs to act. The client no longer needs to interpret startIndex and itemsPerPage or work out the page number itself. We translated the provider’s state into the next action our client could take.
documents.s: 4.2. Turning pagination state into a next action

documents.t: At the time, we did the translation in BookSearchService: Aladin Search API ↓ AladinBookClient ↓ AladinSearchResponse ↓ BookSearchService - Structure the contributor credits - Calculate nextPage - Convert fields ↓ BookSearchResponse ↓ Chaekchaek Client This kept Aladin’s field names and pagination rules out of the client. Inside the backend, though, BookSearchService still depended directly on provider types such as AladinSearchResponse and AladinBookItem. The external contract reached as far as our application service. That was a reasonable trade-off at the time. We had one search provider, and getting search working mattered more. Abstractions have a cost of their own. What I want to understand about a boundary is what it would cost us to make a change with that boundary in place. If adding or replacing a provider became a realistic prospect, we could finish the translation before the response reached the application service: Aladin Search API ↓ Aladin Adapter - Interpret the external contract - Structure the contributor credits - Calculate pagination ↓ BookSearchResult ↓ BookSearchService By the time the service receives the result, it’s already in Chaekchaek’s terms. The service can use it without knowing who supplied it or how they encoded it. The particular interface or adapter pattern is secondary here. Where a boundary belongs can change as the pressures on the system change.

Our AladinContributorParser understands credits like this one: 앤디 위어 (지은이), 박아람 (옮긴이) Its knowledge of labels such as (지은이) and (옮긴이) comes with an assumption: Aladin will keep sending credits in a format we recognize. What if a new role such as 엮은이 appears? What if the same information arrives as 지은이=앤디 위어, ...? A missing JSON field might cause deserialization to fail immediately. The harder case is when the code runs successfully and produces the wrong result. If the parser credits someone as an author by mistake, or silently discards a role it doesn’t recognize, the request can still succeed. The client receives an incorrect result that looks perfectly ordinary. How to detect a change upstream, what to do with a value we can’t interpret, and how much to guard against are questions worth a separate post.
documents.s: 6. A change in the response can break the translation

documents.t: When I started, I pictured the work like this: Aladin response → Put it in a DTO → Pick the fields we need and return them What I ended up doing was different. We read two distinct roles out of a single contributor credit: 앤디 위어 (지은이), 박아람 (옮긴이) ↓ authors: ["앤디 위어"] translators: ["박아람"] We also turned the pagination fields into a value the client could use directly: totalResults + startIndex + itemsPerPage ↓ nextPage Seen from the client’s side, that same change looks like this: Aladin’s pagination data totalResults + startIndex + itemsPerPage ↓ The value the client will use nextPage In both cases, the work was in deciding what the provider’s data meant for our service. That’s what I mean by translation. Original post on Rilog (Korean)
